This page covers the exact US occupation O*NET/SOC 17-2111.00, "Health and Safety Engineers, Except Mining Safety Engineers and Inspectors" (health and safety engineers): promoting workplace or product safety by applying knowledge of industrial processes, mechanics, chemistry, psychology, and industrial health and safety laws. It includes industrial product safety engineers. Original official scope: Promote worksite or product safety by applying knowledge of industrial processes, mechanics, chemistry, psychology, and industrial health and safety laws. Includes industrial product safety engineers. Core tasks listed by O*NET include investigating industrial accidents, injuries, or occupational diseases to determine causes and preventive measures (importance: 88); conducting research to evaluate product safety levels (84); evaluating the safety of product designs (83); conducting or coordinating employee training in safety laws and regulations, hazardous condition monitoring, and safety equipment use (82); maintaining and applying knowledge of current policies, regulations, and industrial processes (82); recommending procedures for detecting, preventing, and eliminating physical, chemical, or other product hazards (82); reporting or reviewing findings from accident investigations, facility inspections, or environmental tests (81); evaluating potential health hazards or damage from product misuse (81); evaluating the adequacy of actions taken to correct health inspection violations (77); interpreting safety regulations for others concerned with industrial safety (74); reviewing plans and specifications for constructing new machinery or equipment to determine whether all safety requirements are met (73); participating in the preparation of product usage and warning label instructions (72); interviewing employers and employees for information about work environments and workplace incidents (70); providing expert testimony in litigation (70); reviewing employee safety programs for adequacy (70); conducting or directing tests of air quality, noise, temperature, or radiation levels to verify compliance with health and safety regulations (70); providing organizations with technical advice and guidance on handling health-related issues and making necessary changes (69); developing industry standards for product safety (65); maintaining liaison with outside organizations, such as fire departments, mutual aid societies, and rescue teams, to facilitate emergency response (65); planning and conducting industrial hygiene research (61); compiling, analyzing, and interpreting statistics related to occupational diseases and accidents (59); writing and revising safety regulations and codes (58); designing and building safety equipment (58); consulting medical professionals to assess health risks and develop methods for managing health issues and concerns (57); and inspecting factory floors to ensure they are strong enough to support heavy machinery (50). Other tasks include inspecting facilities, machinery, or safety equipment to identify and correct potential hazards and ensure compliance with safety regulations, and installing safety devices on machinery or directing equipment installation. Common titles include Health and Safety Specialist, Industrial Hygienist, Industrial Safety Engineer, Product Safety Engineer, Safety Engineer, System Safety Engineer, Product Safety Consultant, and Safety and Health Consultant. Wage, employment, and industry figures on this page use this occupation's own scope as presented on O*NET's 17-2111.00 page, which does not label them as drawn from a parent or broader occupation and shows projected growth for 2024–2034 as "Average (3% to 4%)" (average). See the sections below for scope and boundaries.

Practice scenario | An entirely fictional workplace safety and product safety assessment task package (for practicing the process only; it represents no real business, site, product, incident, client, or data). Draft a plan addressing: (1) how to organize hazard identification, risk assessment, and compliance review using a fictional workplace hazard list and product safety design description, with a structured approach covering hazard categories, exposure routes and affected groups; risk likelihood, severity and priorities; existing controls and applicable regulations and standards; corrective action recommendations, responsibility and deadlines; and residual risks and review methods. Specify information gaps requiring supplementation, including processes, equipment and materials; exposure monitoring data and occupational exposure limits; applicable versions of regulations and standards; intended product use and misuse scenarios; and previous accident and inspection records. (2) How to design completion and review points for a fictional hazard identification, risk assessment, and corrective action tracking form, covering fields and units; hazards, areas, positions and populations; likelihood, severity and risk levels; the hierarchy of controls and responsible persons; deadlines, verification and closure evidence; and original records and revision trails. (3) How to write a safety assessment summary suitable for handover: scope and methods—hazards and risks—compliance with regulations and standards—corrective action recommendations and priorities—residual risks and outstanding items. (4) How to record and retain assessment, monitoring, corrective action, training, and accident investigation records, distinguishing disclosable information from controlled materials or those involving business, employee, or personal information. (5) How to pause, review, and escalate when data are insufficient or assumptions do not hold, corrective actions conflict with regulations, accidents or exposure incidents exceed the assessment scope, or conclusions require statutory qualifications or exceed the role's authority. Use public materials and simulated data; do not use real business data or personally identifying information.

Work context data (percentage of responses) show email at 97%, face-to-face discussions at 93%, telephone conversations at 92%, contact with others at 82%, importance of being exact or accurate at 82%, freedom to make decisions at 81%, impact of decisions on coworkers or company results at 81%, working with or contributing to a work group or team at 81%, responsibility for others' health and safety at 77%, time pressure at 73%, decision frequency at 73%, time spent sitting at 59%, and consequences of error at 57%. If you are willing to base reviews and recommendations on regulations, standards, and data, can communicate with design, production, safety, and compliance stakeholders, and are willing to assume professional responsibility for workplace and product safety, this occupation's daily requirements may align more closely with your working style.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows (17-2111.00, work activity importance scores and work context response percentages) evaluating information to determine compliance with standards (88), getting information (85), evaluating and solving problems (82), and inspecting equipment, structures, or materials (80) as the highest activities. Being exact or accurate is extremely important for 82%; freedom to make decisions is 81%; impact of decisions on coworkers or company results is 81%; responsibility for others' health and safety is very high for 77%; consequences of error are serious for 57%; time pressure occurs every day for 73%; decisions are made every day for 73%; exposure to contaminants occurs every day for 46%; exposure to hazardous conditions occurs every day for 42%; and routine protective equipment is worn every day for 76%. This occupation focuses on workplace hazards, product safety, and industrial hygiene. An error in hazard identification or risk assessment, incorrect application of a regulation or standard, an inaccurate corrective action or verification conclusion, an untruthful accident investigation or data record, or a safety or compliance determination beyond one's authority may cause personal injury, occupational disease, product defects, recalls, and legal liability. O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone Four (considerable preparation needed, SVP 7.0 to less than 8.0), usually requiring a four-year bachelor's degree, though not in every case; the education section on that page does not show a percentage distribution. US projected growth for this occupation on this page in 2024–2034 is "Average (3% to 4%)" (average). If you find it difficult to maintain rigor and objectivity over time while balancing regulations, standards, data, and stakeholder views, to bear high responsibility for others' health and safety and serious consequences of error, or to accept responsibility for the truthfulness of review conclusions and records, treat these as practical costs requiring careful consideration.

Taking responsibility for judgment | Real fit depends on whether you can accomplish several things together in the same safety and product safety assignment: do the professional work thoroughly (use processes, data, regulations, and standards to identify hazards, assess risks, review compliance, recommend and verify corrective actions, cite current versions of standards, and produce usable assessment, corrective action, accident, and training records); manage safety, compliance, and boundaries (review and retain records under occupational safety, product safety, industrial hygiene, fire protection, and environmental requirements; confirm data, assumptions, and standard versions according to procedures; and distinguish disclosable information from controlled materials or those involving business, employee, or personal information and handle them under organizational rules); and accept clearly defined job responsibilities (be accountable for your own assessments, recommendations, and records, and refer matters beyond your authority or involving statutory qualifications, accident determinations, product recalls, compliance determinations, and external disclosures to the appropriate roles or organizations under established rules). Test this through a verifiable experience, such as completing a hazard identification, risk assessment, and compliance review report, a corrective action and verification tracking note, or an investigation review of an accident or exposure incident for a fictional task, rather than relying solely on an interest questionnaire's conclusion.

Direct answer | The health and safety engineers covered here are the exact occupation O*NET 17-2111.00 (Health and Safety Engineers, Except Mining Safety Engineers and Inspectors). Their work falls into several categories: (I) Hazard identification and monitoring—inspect facilities, machinery, or safety equipment to identify and correct potential hazards; conduct or direct tests of air quality, noise, temperature, or radiation levels to verify compliance with health and safety regulations; and inspect factory floors to ensure they are strong enough to support heavy machinery. (II) Risk assessment and compliance review—evaluate the adequacy of actions taken to correct health inspection violations; review plans and specifications for constructing new machinery or equipment to determine whether all safety requirements are met; and maintain and apply knowledge of current policies, regulations, and industrial processes. (III) Corrective action recommendations and standards development—recommend procedures to detect, prevent, and eliminate physical, chemical, or other product hazards; develop industry standards for product safety; write and revise safety regulations and codes; and design and build safety equipment. (IV) Accident investigation and professional support—investigate industrial accidents, injuries, or occupational diseases to determine causes and preventive measures; report or review findings from accident investigations, facility inspections, or environmental tests; provide expert testimony in litigation; and consult medical professionals to assess health risks. (V) Product safety review—conduct research to evaluate product safety levels, evaluate the safety of product designs and potential health hazards or damage from product misuse, and help prepare product usage and warning label instructions. (VI) Training and stakeholder coordination—conduct or coordinate employee training in safety laws and regulations, hazardous condition monitoring, and safety equipment use; review employee safety programs for adequacy; provide organizations with technical advice and guidance on health-related issues; and maintain liaison with outside organizations such as fire departments, mutual aid societies, and rescue teams to facilitate emergency response. The work cycle connects hazard identification and monitoring—risk assessment and compliance review—corrective action recommendations and standards application—accident investigation and professional support—product safety review—training, stakeholder coordination, and review. This page does not conflate this occupation with adjacent environmental compliance inspectors, fire and protection engineers, environmental engineers, environmental scientists and specialists, environmental science and protection technicians, occupational health and safety specialists, occupational health and safety technicians, industrial engineers, or safety management specialists. Nor does it expand health and safety engineering responsibilities to replace statutorily qualified organizations in deciding accident determinations, product recalls, or compliance determinations.

Work and recordkeeping notes | Start with processes, equipment, materials, data, and applicable regulations and standards. Safety, occupational health, and product safety notes | Organize assessments under occupational safety, product safety, industrial hygiene, fire protection, special equipment, and environmental protection requirements. Standards and quality boundaries | This page involves several types of requirements. Professional practice and quality: hazard identification, risk assessment, compliance review, accident investigation, and product safety review must follow processes, data, and current regulations and standards, with monitoring, corrective action, and accident records maintained. Controlled materials or those involving business, employee, or personal information, as well as externally disclosed information, must be managed through approval and minimum-necessary access. Records and collaboration | Under organizational safety, product safety, and compliance management rules, record hazards, areas, positions and populations; likelihood, severity and risk levels; control hierarchy, responsible persons and deadlines; monitoring and testing data and methods; accident timelines, evidence and cause analysis; corrective action verification and closure evidence; and training and qualification information, using prescribed templates and deadlines. Immediately pause when data are insufficient or assumptions do not hold, regulation or standard versions are uncertain, an immediate hazard exists on site, an accident or exposure exceeds the assessment scope, or records differ from on-site conditions. Escalate within your authority and request review by safety, compliance, legal, and medical roles. Do not modify records or add entries retrospectively on your own authority.

Boundary conclusion | This page covers O*NET 17-2111.00 (Health and Safety Engineers). The core differences from adjacent roles lie in subjects, outputs, and levels of authority. This occupation focuses on identifying and assessing workplace hazards, product safety, and industrial hygiene, compliance review, and accident investigation. Its outputs are records of hazard identification, risk assessment, compliance review, corrective action recommendations, accident investigation, and product safety review completed under current regulations and standards. Authority for statutory qualification determinations, accident conclusions, product recalls, and compliance determinations cannot be transferred across roles.

Cross-disciplinary conclusions and those involving statutory determinations, recalls, penalties, or legal use have limits on their applicability.

This occupation's conclusion boundaries | Assessment and monitoring conclusions state only verifiable hazards, exposure, data, methods, versions of regulations and standards, and corrective action and verification records, distinguishing measured facts, judgments and inferences, and matters awaiting verification. Do not make unauthorized judgments or commitments on matters beyond your authority (statutory qualification determinations, accident investigation conclusions, product recalls, compliance determinations, and external disclosures). paragraphs: Conclusion | The core differences between this occupation (O*NET 17-2111.00, Health and Safety Engineers) and adjacent roles lie in subjects, outputs, and levels of authority. This occupation focuses on identifying and assessing workplace hazards, product safety, and industrial hygiene, compliance review, and accident investigation, producing records of hazard identification, risk assessment, compliance review, corrective action recommendations, accident investigation, and product safety review under current regulations and standards. Occupational Health and Safety Specialists (19-5011.00) focus on implementing occupational health and safety procedures, on-site compliance, and training; Fire-Prevention and Protection Engineers (17-2111.02) on fire and protection system design reviews; Environmental Compliance Inspectors (13-1041.01) on environmental regulatory compliance inspections and evidence collection; Industrial Engineers (17-2112.00) on production systems, processes, and efficiency optimization; and Security Management Specialists (13-1199.07) on organizational security policies, risk management, and incident response. Their subjects, outputs, and levels of authority differ. Authority for statutory qualification determinations, accident conclusions, product recalls, and compliance determinations cannot be carried across roles.

They do not establish qualification, hiring, or pay conclusions, nor constitute occupational safety, product safety, industrial hygiene, medical, legal, or compliance advice. Introduction | The following comparison uses four columns: career track—core work and outputs—key differences—which choice is a better fit. Workplace safety, product safety, industrial hygiene, occupational health, fire protection, and compliance often connect within the same manufacturing or service organization, but connection does not imply interchangeability. When moving between tracks, learn the new track's subjects, regulations, standards, data, authorization, and responsibility boundaries.

Key differences: this occupation focuses on identifying and assessing workplace hazards, product safety, and industrial hygiene, compliance review, and accident investigation. It assesses and recommends within its authority based on processes, data, and current regulations and standards, taking responsibility for safety, compliance, and records. Other roles center on occupational health procedure implementation, fire and protection system design, environmental regulatory compliance inspections, production system optimization, or organizational security management. They usually have more specialized rules, subjects, and authorization requirements and do not bear primary responsibility for product safety reviews, accident cause analysis, and compliance determinations (but must collaborate with this occupation and clarify boundaries).

Better suited to people willing to base reviews and recommendations on regulations, standards, and data, communicate with design, production, safety, and compliance stakeholders, and accept professional responsibility for workplace and product safety.

Core work and outputs: inspect facilities, machinery, and safety equipment to identify and correct potential hazards; conduct or direct air, noise, temperature, and radiation tests to verify compliance; evaluate the adequacy of corrective actions and design specifications; investigate industrial accidents, injuries, and occupational diseases to determine causes and preventive measures; review product safety and potential hazards from misuse; develop industry standards for product safety and write and revise safety regulations and codes; conduct employee safety training and provide technical advice on health issues. Outputs are records of hazard identification, risk assessment, compliance review, corrective action recommendations, accident investigation, and product safety review completed under current regulations and standards (O*NET/SOC 17-2111.00).
This occupation: Health and Safety Engineers (O*NET/SOC 17-2111.00, Health and Safety Engineers, Except Mining Safety Engineers and Inspectors)

Key differences: occupational health and safety specialists focus on implementing occupational health and safety procedures, site inspections, training, and compliance records, producing procedure implementation, inspection, and training records. This occupation focuses on hazard identification, risk assessment, compliance review, accident investigation, and product safety review based on processes and data, producing assessment, review, and investigation records. On-site safety procedure implementation and workstation inspections are usually not its primary duties (but it must collaborate with occupational health and safety specialists and distinguish review from implementation).

Better suited to people who want to implement occupational health and safety procedures, inspect sites, and provide training; this occupation emphasizes hazard identification, risk assessment, compliance review, and accident investigation.

Core work and outputs: conduct site inspections, workstation assessments, training, and compliance recordkeeping under occupational health and safety procedures; track corrective actions and address site safety issues. Outputs are procedure implementation, inspection, and training records.
Occupational Health and Safety Specialists (19-5011.00)

Key differences: fire-prevention and protection engineers focus on fire and protection system design reviews and applications of fire science, producing protection system designs and review opinions. This occupation focuses on comprehensive assessment of workplace hazards, product safety, and industrial hygiene and on accident investigation, producing assessment, review, and investigation records. It usually does not bear primary responsibility for protection system design and fire science calculations (but must collaborate with fire-prevention and protection engineers and distinguish system design from comprehensive assessment).

Better suited to people who want to design and review fire and protection systems; this occupation emphasizes comprehensive assessment of workplace hazards and product safety and accident investigation.

Core work and outputs: design and review fire prevention, detection, suppression, and evacuation systems under fire codes and fire science, and perform calculations and verification. Outputs are protection system designs and review opinions.
Fire-Prevention and Protection Engineers (17-2111.02)

Key differences: environmental compliance inspectors focus on environmental regulatory compliance inspections, evidence collection, and corrective action requirements, producing inspection conclusions, corrective action requirements, and evidence collection records. This occupation focuses on workplace hazard, product safety, and industrial hygiene assessment, producing assessment, review, and investigation records. It usually does not bear primary responsibility for environmental enforcement or administrative penalties (but must collaborate with environmental compliance inspectors and distinguish inspections and enforcement from professional assessment).

Better suited to people who want to conduct environmental regulatory compliance inspections, collect evidence, and support enforcement; this occupation emphasizes professional assessment of workplace hazards and product safety and compliance recommendations.

Core work and outputs: inspect, monitor, and collect evidence under environmental regulations and emission standards, and issue corrective action requirements and inspection conclusions. Outputs are inspection conclusions, corrective action requirements, and evidence collection records.
Environmental Compliance Inspectors (13-1041.01)

Key differences: industrial engineers focus on optimizing production systems, processes, capacity, and efficiency, producing process and capacity optimization plans and efficiency metrics. This occupation focuses on assessing and controlling workplace hazards and product safety, producing assessment, review, and investigation records. It usually does not bear primary responsibility for production system efficiency or capacity design (but must collaborate with industrial engineers to incorporate safety requirements into processes and designs).
Better suited to people who want to optimize production systems, processes, and efficiency; this occupation emphasizes workplace hazard and product safety assessment and compliance review.

Core work and outputs: use statistics, operations research, and engineering methods to analyze processes, human-machine interactions, and logistics, and design improvement plans and performance metrics. Outputs are process, capacity, and efficiency optimization plans.
Industrial Engineers (17-2112.00)

Key differences: security management specialists focus on organizational security policies, risk management, incident response, and security culture, producing security policy, risk management, and incident response documents. This occupation focuses on hazard identification, risk assessment, and product safety review based on processes, data, regulations, and standards, producing assessment, review, and investigation records. It usually does not bear primary responsibility for organizational security policymaking, information security, or risk management systems (but must collaborate with security management specialists and distinguish professional review from organizational management).

Better suited to people who want to work on organizational security policies, risk management, and incident response; this occupation emphasizes professional assessment of workplace hazards and product safety and compliance review.

Core work and outputs: develop and implement organizational security policies, risk management, incident response, security training, and audits. Outputs are security policy, risk management, and incident response documents and audit records.
Security Management Specialists (13-1199.07)

Occupational definition | The health and safety engineers covered here are the exact occupation O*NET 17-2111.00 (Health and Safety Engineers, Except Mining Safety Engineers and Inspectors): promoting workplace or product safety by applying knowledge of industrial processes, mechanics, chemistry, psychology, and industrial health and safety laws. Direct answer | The core occupational risk is not merely whether problems can be identified, but four types of failure with serious consequences. Safety and health failure: missed hazards, exposure assessment errors, or failed controls can cause injury and occupational disease; inadequate protection during site inspection and monitoring or failure to identify chemical, physical, biological, radiation, mechanical, and other hazards may cause injury and occupational health harm. Compliance and liability failure: applying incorrect regulation or standard versions, failing to implement corrective action recommendations or adequately verify them, or inaccurate accident investigations or data records may cause violations, penalties, legal liability, product defects, and recalls. Conclusion and verification failure: incorrect risk classification, inaccurate accident cause analysis, unreliable product safety conclusions, or insufficient corrective action closure evidence may cause rework, residual risks, and misjudgments. Authorization and collaboration failure: independently issuing compliance determinations, accident conclusions, product recall recommendations, or external disclosures beyond authorization; reliance on a single point for critical qualifications or testing capabilities; and unclear standards for responsibility, corrective actions, and disclosure with production, design, legal, and regulatory stakeholders can cause disputes. O*NET data—being exact or accurate is extremely important for 82%, responsibility for others' health and safety is very high for 77%, decisions have important effects on coworkers or company results for 81%, and consequences of error are serious for 57%—provide occupational grounds for the seriousness of these risk consequences.

entries.answer: The health and safety engineers covered here are the exact occupation O*NET 17-2111.00 (Health and Safety Engineers, Except Mining Safety Engineers and Inspectors): promoting workplace or product safety by applying knowledge of industrial processes, mechanics, chemistry, psychology, and industrial health and safety laws. It includes industrial product safety engineers. Core tasks include investigating industrial accidents, injuries, and occupational diseases to determine causes and preventive measures (importance: 88); researching product safety levels (84); evaluating product design safety (83); conducting or coordinating employee training (82); maintaining and applying knowledge of current policies, regulations, and industrial processes (82); recommending hazard detection, prevention, and elimination procedures (82); reporting or reviewing investigation and inspection findings (81); evaluating potential health hazards from product misuse (81); evaluating corrective action adequacy (77); interpreting safety regulations (74); reviewing machinery or equipment plans and specifications (73); and conducting or directing air, noise, temperature, and radiation tests (70). Common titles include Health and Safety Specialist, Industrial Hygienist, Industrial Safety Engineer, Product Safety Engineer, Safety Engineer, and System Safety Engineer. O*NET's 17-2111.00 page shows the main US industries as professional, scientific, and technical services and manufacturing. This page describes the US occupational classification scope; wages and employment use this occupation's own scope (17-2111.00). entries.answer: The core differences lie in subjects, outputs, and levels of authority. This occupation focuses on identifying and assessing workplace hazards, product safety, and industrial hygiene, compliance review, and accident investigation, producing records of hazard identification, risk assessment, compliance review, corrective action recommendations, accident investigation, and product safety review under current regulations and standards. Occupational Health and Safety Specialists (19-5011.00) focus on occupational health and safety procedure implementation and site inspections; Fire-Prevention and Protection Engineers (17-2111.02) on fire and protection system design reviews; Environmental Compliance Inspectors (13-1041.01) on environmental regulatory compliance inspections and evidence collection; Environmental Engineers (17-2081.00) on environmental engineering design; Environmental Scientists and Specialists (19-2041.00) and Environmental Science and Protection Technicians (19-4042.00) on environmental science and monitoring; Industrial Engineers (17-2112.00) on production systems and efficiency optimization; and Security Management Specialists (13-1199.07) on organizational security policies and risk management. Their subjects, activities, and levels of authority differ. Authority for statutory qualification determinations, accident conclusions, product recalls, and compliance determinations cannot be carried across roles.

subject.summary: Health and Safety Engineers, Except Mining Safety Engineers and Inspectors corresponds to the exact occupation O*NET/SOC 17-2111.00, "Health and Safety Engineers, Except Mining Safety Engineers and Inspectors": promoting workplace or product safety by applying knowledge of industrial processes, mechanics, chemistry, psychology, and industrial health and safety laws. It includes industrial product safety engineers. Core tasks include investigating industrial accidents and occupational diseases, evaluating product designs and misuse risks, conducting or directing tests of air, noise, temperature, and radiation, evaluating the adequacy of corrective actions, reviewing machinery and equipment plans and specifications, and providing employee safety training. Common job titles include Health and Safety Specialist, Industrial Hygienist, Industrial Safety Engineer, Product Safety Engineer, and Safety Engineer. Original official scope: Promote worksite or product safety by applying knowledge of industrial processes, mechanics, chemistry, psychology, and industrial health and safety laws. Includes industrial product safety engineers. Scope note: US wage and employment data on this page use this occupation's own scope (17-2111.00) as presented by O*NET on its 17-2111.00 page (which does not label the data as drawn from a parent occupation); figures from adjacent occupations are not substituted. Projected growth for this occupation in 2024–2034 is 3% to 4%, and O*NET places it in Job Zone Four (considerable preparation needed, SVP 7.0 to less than 8.0). This page does not constitute occupational safety, product safety, industrial hygiene, medical, legal, or compliance advice.
